newsitem.title: UK: Morgan Grenfell acts to restore MGAM reputation.
newsitem.headline: Morgan Grenfell acts to restore MGAM reputation.

text.p: Deutsche Morgan Grenfell on Wednesday confirmed the sacrifice of four key managers in an attempt to restore faith in its troubled asset management group, still reeling from last month's revelations of mis-valuations in three of its funds and the sacking of fund manager Peter Young.

The investment banking arm of Germany's mighty Deutsche Bank said Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) head Keith Percy would leave and be replaced by Robert Smith, head of development capital and the man chosen earlier to lead an internal investigation into what went wrong at the funds.

Percy, along with directors Glyn Owen, Graham Kane and Michael Wheatley will all leave the firm under the terms of their contracts. Owen was MGAM's chief investment officer and Young's immediate boss, Wheatley was compliance director and Kane headed MGAM's unit trust business.

"Our internal investigations have revealed management failings, which contributed to the problems in our unit trust business and these changes have been made as a result," DMG chief executive Michael Dobson said.
The departures follow revelations of major problems in three MGAM funds last month. The discovery of mis-valuations of speculative unlisted stocks led to their temporary suspension.

Trading in the funds, which were held by around 90,000 retail investors, resumed after Deutsche Bank stepped in with a 180 million pound ($285.3 million) cash injection to shore them up. It later vowed to support the funds for at least three months and to compensate investors for any losses.

Young, who is currently being investigated by Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO), has said he is not guilty of any criminal activity and is being made a scapegoat for failings. He was dismissed on the grounds of alleged "gross misconduct".
DMG also said in a statement that a senior associate director, Paul Ebling, will leave the firm. Apart from Smith, it did not name replacements for any of the managers.

Robert Smith, a 52-year-old Scotsman, said the internal inquiry was largely complete and MGAM would continue to work with Britain's investments watchdog the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO) and other regulators "to resolve outstanding issues".

IMRO is conducting its own investigation into the funds and is not expected to report on its findings for some months. If the regulator finds MGAM breached the rules, it could lead to hefty fines and possible action against individuals.
Smith reiterated a pledge that investors would not be left short-changed by the problems in the funds.
"If compensation is found to be due under IMRO rules or other legislation, we will pay it," Smith said.

He said the priority was to restore MGAM's reputation in the unit trust business and said he was determined that MGAM would continue to deliver "superior performance for clients in virtually every asset class".

There has been intense speculation over whether Percy would resign, with some reports that influential MGAM clients had threatened to withdraw assets if he was fired, while others were reported to be unhappy if he stayed.
Deutsche Bank has said since the beginning of the debacle that those with immediate responsibility for Young's activities would not continue to work for the group.

But obvious internal regret at their departure was evident in Dobson's statement in which he paid tribute to the "major contribution to our asset management business over many years" made by the five men who are leaving.
Dobson said Smith was the natural choice to take on the leadership of the business. ($1=.6309 Pound)
